newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia food prices seen rising on rupiah crisis.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia food prices seen rising on rupiah crisis.

text.p: Prices of food items ranging from chicken and meat to noodles are expected to increase as Indonesia reels from a currency crisis that has clipped some 25 percent of the rupiah's value, traders said on Tuesday.

"The higher cost of importing raw materials used to produce food items has to be passed on to the consumer," one trader said. "We will be seeing an increase in the prices of items such as chicken, meat and noodles."
All of the wheat used in making noodles, popular as a snack or a meal among Indonesians who are moving away from rice as their incomes grow, is imported as Indonesia does not grow wheat.
Indonesia, the world's fourth-most populous country with more than 200 million people, also imports corn and soymeal, which are used to feed poultry and cattle.
"About 400,000 to 450,000 tonnes of corn imported by Indonesian feedmills and traders are either afloat or will arrive in September," one trader said.

"Their cost has gone up by more than 20 percent since they were purchased because of the rupiah," he said, adding that most local buyers choose to pay when they take delivery at the then prevailing exchange rate.
"The profit margins, especially of traders, is nowhere near 20 percent. So they will have to pass on the cost to consumers, although not the whole 20 percent," he added.
The rupiah began its descent against the U.S. dollar in early July following fierce speculative offshore attacks on the currency, when it was hovering around 2,430 to the dollar.
It had fallen to 2,980/3,000 at 0500 GMT on Tuesday, but recovered to 2,900/2,920 at 0700 GMT.
"Prices of food products made from imported raw materials have to be revised upwards," one trader said. "I think the change will take place within weeks."
He said existing stocks of imported raw materials such as corn and soymeal could be replaced within a month.
"Once inventories are depleted and they have to be replaced, the new exchange rate comes into play," he added. "This is the time we will see an explosion in prices."
Traders also said the import problem had been compounded by an expected smaller corn harvest in East Java due, in part, to the drought sweeping across the archipelago.

"Arrivals usually start from June, but this has not been the case this year," one trader said. "My expectation is that the harvest will only be about 40 percent of the usual 300,000 to 400,000 tonnes we get."
He said the smaller harvest was also due to farmers switching to more profitable crops such as sugar cane and soybeans.
Beddu Amang, chairman of Indonesia's commodities regulator BULOG, said on Thursday prices of essential foodstuff such as cooking oil, rice, sugar and soybeans were mostly stable.
BULOG has 3.0 million tonnes of rice stocks, and there is no need for imports, he told reporters after meeting President Suharto, who takes a personal interest in food prices.
Traders said corn prices were slightly higher at 440 rupiah/kg in Jakarta, compared with 420-430 rupiah a week ago, while soymeal prices were at 910 rupiah against 880-890 rupiah.
